results.summary: This project is an interactive Morse code trainer that displays letters on a 7-segment display and challenges the user to enter the correct Morse pattern using a switch. It provides immediate feedback through a correct-result output and progresses through the English alphabet. The design is intended for simulation or hardware testing, with a start input and a Morse input pin. The documentation is brief and does not describe the full testing procedure or external hardware requirements in detail.

This is a simple gate test project created in Wokwi that lets the user experiment with different logic gates by toggling switches. Some inputs and outputs are interconnected between gates, and the user tries to achieve a specific outcome. It requires external switches and a single-digit LED display for interaction. The documentation is minimal and does not specify the exact logic function or expected behavior.

This design displays a bouncing ROOTS logo with an animated color gradient and a kaleidoscope background on a VGA monitor. It is configured through input pins and requires a Tiny VGA Pmod for connection to a VGA display. The project is written in Verilog and runs at a 25.175 MHz clock. The documentation is limited to a brief description and does not include detailed testing or configuration instructions.

This project implements a variable-length LFSR with selectable 2-tap or 4-tap configurations, along with hold and step control signals. It outputs the low-order 15 bits of the LFSR value and a valid signal indicating whether the selected configuration is supported. The design was tested using hand-generated test modules and GTK signal evaluation, but no automated test is included. External hardware is not required beyond setting the input pins to configure the LFSR.

Borg is a tiny GPU built around a RISC-V SoC (TinyQV) that renders a 10-frame animation of a rotating RGB triangle entirely from firmware. It includes vertex shading, rasterization, and RGB fragment shading, and communicates via UART and QSPI interfaces. Testing is done on an FPGA using a make target that programs the firmware and reads back PPM images. External hardware includes a QSPI Pmod and, for FPGA development, a pico-ice board and Raspberry Pi Debug Probe.

This chip is a character-level transformer language model with ternary weights baked into ROM that generates Shakespeare-style text. It streams int16 residuals in and int8 residuals out over a byte protocol, with the host handling character and position tables and final sampling. The design requires a host microcontroller (RP2350B on the Tiny Tapeout demo board) to drive the protocol and clock the chip, and it can be tested with reference firmware or a simple logic analyser test. Notable features include the entire model stored in 4,480 bytes of ROM and a 5-lane arithmetic unit that processes five weights per byte.

This project implements a simplified 8-bit microprocessor inspired by the 6502 architecture, featuring an ALU, registers, and a microcoded instruction decoder for a subset of the 6502 instruction set. It exposes data and address pins for external memory and I/O, and is intended for simulation or hardware testing. The documentation describes two testing strategies but does not provide a complete test program or external hardware list. The design is a custom educational processor rather than a cycle-accurate reproduction.

This Wokwi project is a Morse code generator circuit for the letters J and R, using a 4-bit synchronous counter and logic gates to produce dot and dash patterns. It can be tested by connecting a 7-segment display and using a button to select between the two letters. External hardware includes a button, a 7-segment display, and a clock. The documentation is brief and does not include a schematic or detailed explanation of the logic.

DUMBRV is a small RISC-V processor supporting the RV32E base instruction set plus Zicond and Zbs extensions, using two independent SPI memory ports for instruction and data storage. It provides 8 GPIO inputs and 8 GPIO outputs, and requires external SPI ROM and RAM with 2-byte addressing. The processor starts execution from address 0x0 and can be tested with a provided program that records GPIO inputs and outputs them after a delay. The design is notable for its minimalistic approach and reliance on external SPI memories.

This project attempts to build a random number generator using the unstable state of a latch when both set and reset are held low. It includes 34 instances per output pin to increase the chance of at least one working random source, and the input pins select which instance to observe. The design can be frozen to sample a value, but the author notes it may not work due to bias or constant outputs. The documentation is informal and the project is highly experimental with no guaranteed randomness.
